newsitem.title: USA: New York State battles frivolous inmate lawsuits.
newsitem.headline: New York State battles frivolous inmate lawsuits.

text.p: A New York inmate is suing the state for causing amnesia he says made him wander away from prison, another inmate is suing over losing weight on a jailhouse diet, and now state officials say they've had enough.
State Attorney General Dennis Vacco on Monday declared war on frivolous lawsuits filed by inmates, complaining that the 7,700 lawsuits filed last year alone are clogging the system.
The courts dismiss about 95 percent of all inmate lawsuits, which cost the state an estimated $80 million a year, Vacco said. He offered his list of the "Top Five" most frivolous cases:

Francis Hugh Smith, a burglar with a rap sheet spanning five decades, claims New York owes him $10 million because faulty medical care caused amnesia that made him leave his work release job and forget to return to prison.
Brooklyn burglar Anthony Malloy sought "$989 billion trillion" because he said prison guards beat up his jacket, which he was not wearing at the time. His case was dismissed.
Convicted killer Anthony Gill claims second-hand cigarette smoke from other inmates is causing him medical problems, although he buys cigarettes from the prison commissary.
Jose Reyes, convicted of burglary, wants $1,000 because the state made him eat "vegetable diet" loaf as discipline for violating prison rules and he lost one pound.

Thomas Higgins, who sodomized and killed two children who stumbled upon a 1978 robbery, sued the state for $10,000 because a prison laundry machine broke and he claims a constitutional right to clean clothes and blankets.
"These ridiculous lawsuits are just a sample of the many meritless, frivolous cases filed by inmates that clog our courts and waste taxpayers' resources," Vacco said.
The number of lawsuits filed last year was up 32 percent over 1995, when frivolous cases included complaints over soapy milk, bad haircuts and melted ice cream, he said.

Vacco proposed reforms such as requiring prisoners to pay a $50 filing fee, exhaust all their administrative remedies and be subject to sanctions for filing such suits. The proposed reforms will be considered by the state legislature.
